With the FinOps Customization API, customers can adapt the dimensions of their billing data to their
specific needs. This flexibility provides a more granular view of cost and usage data, supporting precise and insightful
financial analysis.

| Zone        | Base URL    |
| ----------- | ----------- |
| NAM         | https://api.flexera.com/finops-customizations |
| EU          | https://api.flexera.eu/finops-customizations  |
| APAC        | https://api.flexera.au/finops-customizations  |

tags.description:
See: [https://docs.flexera.com/flexera/EN/Optima/OptimaRuleBasedDimensions.htm](https://docs.flexera.com/flexera/EN/Optima/OptimaRuleBasedDimensions.htm)

This API lets you create new dimensions that will be populated according to rules you define.
You can use these new dimensions to look at your costs from new, meaningful perspectives.

A common use case is to create several dimensions like **Department** or **Environment**, populated based on known account values.
You might define a **Department** rule-based dimension with a rule for each known account.
For instance, a rule might express: "If the account is 'aws-123', then use the value 'Finance'".
In that way, all the "aws-123" costs will be classified as being in the "Finance" Department.

## API

There are three paths for managing rule-based dimensions, under `/finops-customizations/v1/orgs/{orgId}`:
  - `/rule-based-dimensions`: List all rule-based dimensions.
  - `/rule-based-dimensions/{id}`: Show, create, update, delete a single rule-based dimension.
  - `/rule-based-dimensions/{id}/rules/{effectiveAt}`: Show, replace, delete a single rules list.

Each rule-based dimension has an `id` and a display `name`.
It can also have rule lists describing how to populate the dimension over time.

There is a prototype rules list UI where you can paste in JSON on the left and view/edit a human-readable version on the right:
- [Rule List JSON Editor](https://reference.rightscale.com/bill_analysis/rbd_json_editor/index.html)

### Rule List

A rule list describes how a rule-based dimension should be populated.
A rule simply has a `condition` and a `value`.
As each line of your bill data is gathered, the rules will be evaluated in order and the first rule to match will determine the value to populate for that row.

The `value` field can specify either:
- A static text value (using `text`), or
- A dynamic value from another dimension (using `dimension`). 
		
Here are example rules demonstrating different `value` configurations:

#### Example 1: Static Text Value
This rule says: if the vendor account is AWS, populate the rule-based dimension with the static value "Finance":
~~~~
{
 "condition": {
   "type":      "dimension_equals",
   "dimension": "vendor",
   "value":     "AWS"
 },
 "value": {
   "text": "Finance"
 }
}
~~~~
The next rule demonstrates a dimension_contains condition.

The rule says: If a resource type contains the substring "Compute", populate the rule-based dimension with the value "Finance":
~~~~
{
 "condition": {
   "type":      "dimension_contains",
   "dimension": "resource_type",
   "substring": "Compute"
 },
 "value": {
   "text": "Finance"
 }
}
~~~~
If you're populating a dimension based on 100 different accounts, your rules list might have 100 rules similar to that one, specifying the value to use for each of the 100 accounts.

#### Example 2: Dynamic Dimension Value
This rule says: if the "tag_department" is not empty or "None", populate the rule-based dimension with the value of the "tag_department":
~~~~
{
  "condition": {
    "type": "not",
    "expression": {
      "type": "or",
      "expressions": [
        {
          "type": "dimension_equals",
          "dimension": "tag_department",
          "value": "None",
          "caseInsensitive": false
        },
        {
          "type": "dimension_equals",
          "dimension": "tag_department",
          "value": ""
        }
      ]
    }
  },
  "value": {
    "dimension":  "tag_department",
  }
}
~~~~

#### Rule Condition

A rule's condition could be:
- The `dimension_equals` or `dimension_contains` type
- A boolean operator type: `and`, `or`, `not`
- Empty (null), meaning the rule will match unconditionally

A `dimension_equals` condition checks whether a dimension equals a certain value and a `dimension_contains` condition checks whether a dimension contains a certain substring.
Most dimensions are available to be referenced:
- Default dimensions:
  - `availability_zone`
  - `bill_entity`
  - `bill_source`
  - `billing_account`
  - `commitment_id`
  - `commitment_name`
  - `database_edition`
  - `database_engine`
  - `deployment_option`
  - `description`
  - `instance_type`
  - `instance_type_family`
  - `invoice_id`
  - `license_model`
  - `line_item_type`
  - `manufacturer_name`
  - `meter_category`
  - `operating_system`
  - `product_order_name`
  - `purchase_option`
  - `region`
  - `resource_group`
  - `resource_type`
  - `service`
  - `service_family`
  - `usage_type`
  - `usage_unit`
  - `vendor`
  - `vendor_account`
  - `vendor_account_name`
- Any custom tag dimensions
- Any other rule-based dimensions (as long as the reference doesn't create a circular dependency among the rule-based dimensions)

By default, the condition is case-sensitive, but it can be made case-insensitive by setting its `caseInsensitive` field to `true`.
This applies to both  "dimension_equals" and "dimension_contains"  condition types.
For example:

~~~~
{
  "type": "dimension_equals",
  "dimension": "vendor",
  "value": "AWS",
  "caseInsensitive": true
}
~~~~

A rule's condition could also be more complex, using the boolean operators `and`, `or`, or `not` to build a larger, nested expression.
For example:

_"vendor is AWS **and** service is EC2":_
~~~~
{
 "type": "and",
 "expressions": [
   {"type":"dimension_equals", "dimension":"vendor",  "value":"AWS"},
   {"type":"dimension_equals", "dimension":"service", "value":"EC2"}
 ]
}
~~~~

_"vendor is **not** Azure":_
~~~~
{
 "type": "not",
 "expression": {
   "type":"dimension_equals", "dimension":"vendor", "value":"Azure"
 }
}
~~~~

Rule conditions must use the underlying cost dimension values, not UI display labels.
Some UI surfaces show friendlier names for display.
For example, the displayed vendor name "Google" may correspond to the underlying vendor value "GCP", which is the value the rule must use.
If a dimension is not offered as a dropdown in the rule editor, inspect your cost data to determine the exact raw values present in your org.

### Rules can change over time
The rules for a rule-based dimension are able to change over various time periods — you could define a fresh rules list for each calendar month, if desired.

Each rules list has an `effectiveAt` date, indicating the year-month when the list starts being applicable. 
It remains in effect until a new rules list is added with a subsequent `effectiveAt` date.

For example, a rules list might take effect in "2022-01" (January). Those rules remain in effect from that month forward, until another rules list is defined for a subsequent month.
You might then add a rules list effective "2023-04" (April) and those rules would then be used for that month forward.

### Quotas
An org may define up to 50 rule-based dimensions. And each dimension may define up to 48 rules lists, meaning the rules list can change over time (at 48 unique "effectiveAt" dates).

A single rules list for any dimension may contain up to 500 rules, normally.
To limit the complexity of the condition expressions, there may be 500 condition elements (whether of type "dimension_equals","dimension_contains", "and", "or", or "not") used across the entire list. That means a list might have 500 simple "dimension_equals"/"dimension_contains" rules, or on the other extreme, might only be allowed to have one rule if that rule contains 500 condition elements (for example, a large "or" expression with 499 "dimension_equals"/"dimension_contains" checks).

#### Special Case
There is also a special case on the number of rules: if a list consists of rules that simply check the value of the same dimension (or set of dimensions), we can optimize that and can allow up to 40,000 rules in that list.

A common use case would be to populate a rule-based dimension entirely based on the value of the "vendor_account" dimension.
For instance, you might know the "Department" that should be assigned for every possible account value.
The rules list could support mapping up to 40,000 "vendor_account" values that exist in the org, following this format:
~~~
"rules": [
 {
   "condition": {"type":"dimension_equals", "dimension":"vendor_account", "value":"account_1"},
   "value": {"text": "Finance"}
 },
 {
   "condition": {"type":"dimension_equals", "dimension":"vendor_account", "value":"account_2"},
   "value": {"text": "Engineering"}
 },
 ...<up to 39,998 more rules like the two above>...
]
~~~
This same optimization also applies for rules that check the value of multiple dimensions.
As long as each rule consists of an `and` expression that checks the value of up to 8 dimensions, we can optimize that mapping and support up to 40,000 rules in that list.
Each of those rules must be checking the same set of dimensions, for example all the rules might check both the "vendor_account" and "resource_group" dimensions.

Across all rule-based dimensions, a single effective month may have a maximum of 400,000 applicable rules in total.
## Rule-Based Dimension for Billing Center Allocation

This section outlines the use of a special rule-based dimension, `rbd_bc`, as a powerful alternative to traditional [billing center allocation rules](https://docs.flexera.com/flexera/EN/Optima/Allocation_Rules.htm).

### Advantages of `rbd_bc`

Compared to traditional allocation rules, using `rbd_bc` provides the following benefits:
- Enables the rules to change over time, allowing a different rules list for each month.
- Provides the ability to reference other dimensions that are unavailable to traditional allocation rules, such as other rule-based dimensions, custom tag dimensions, and most built-in dimensions.
- Simplifies the allocation process because one rules list directly assigns costs to leaf-node billing centers, whereas traditional allocation rules require separate rules lists at each level of the hierarchy.

### How to Use `rbd_bc`

To use `rbd_bc` for billing center allocation, follow these steps:

1. Create a rule-based dimension `rbd_bc` which will take over assigning billing center allocations.
   - The `id` must be `rbd_bc`.
   - The `name` can be anything, like "BC", or "Assign to BC", etc. Like any other rule-based dimension, it will be visible in the UI.
1. Choose an `effectiveAt` date for the first rules list. This controls a one-way switchover: starting on that date, the traditional billing center allocation rules will be overridden by this rule-based dimension’s assignments.
1. Create a rules lists that assign costs to a "leaf-node" billing center ID, for example:

       IF vendor_account = "account1" THEN "bc123"

   The end result is that `rbd_bc` will be populated with the ID of the billing center to assign to.
   And the billing center should be a leaf node in the hierarchy, allowing you to freely assign to a billing center several layers down.

#### Example `rbd_bc` Configuration

Here’s an example configuration to create the `rbd_bc` dimension:
~~~
{
  "id": "rbd_bc",
  "name": "Assign to BC"
}
~~~
And we might create a rules list effective `2023-01`, with two rules that assign an account to a specific billing center
(this rules list can be pasted into the [prototype editor UI](https://reference.rightscale.com/bill_analysis/rbd_json_editor/index.html) for further editing):
~~~
[
  {
    "condition": {
      "type": "dimension_equals",
      "dimension": "vendor_account",
      "value": "798380790996"
    },
    "value": {
      "text": "dmsP6WK7qL6yiluIl_3iOQ"
    }
  },
  {
    "condition": {
      "type": "dimension_equals",
      "dimension": "vendor_account",
      "value": "594348054263"
    },
    "value": {
      "text": "YbPKQSkO_qoE6hJ8nx9vkg"
    }
  }
]
~~~
The next time costs are imported, the billing center assignments will be driven by the `rbd_bc` values, starting on its earliest effectiveAt date (`2023-01` in this example).
The traditional billing center allocation rules will only affect dates before this `rbd_bc` effectiveAt date.

### `rbd_bc` for Recommendations

The `rbd_bc` dimension will also override billing center allocation on [savings recommendations](https://docs.flexera.com/flexeraone/EN/WhatsNew/FeatureList/CCORecommendations.htm). This works by internally populating the rule-based dimensions (RBDs) on each recommendation and using the `rbd_bc` value to allocate the recommendation to a billing center.

However, recommendations are separate from cost data and only have two fields available for RBD rules to reference:
- `vendor_account`
- `resource_group`

Any RBD rules checking the recommendation's account or resource group should work, for example:
- `IF vendor_account == "A" THEN "bc123"`
- `IF resource_group == "B" THEN "bc456"`

If an RBD rule checks the value of an unsupported dimension, such as `bill_source == "X"`, that clause will evaluate to false because the recommendation doesn't have a `bill_source` field.

But a rule containing an unsupported dimension could still match if it contained an `OR` expression.
Consider the following example rule condition that checks two fields:
```
bill_source == "X" OR vendor_account == "A"
```

Since `bill_source` doesn't exist on recommendations, the `bill_source == "X"` clause evaluates to false. However, the overall rule can still match if `vendor_account == "A"`.

tags.description:
The Tag Dimensions APIs allow any resource tags (or "labels" in Google Cloud Platform) in your bill data to be enabled
as custom dimensions, which helps in grouping resources and analyzing the cloud bill data.

This API exposes methods to create, read, update and delete tag dimensions.

See
[Tag Dimensions](https://docs.flexera.com/flexera/EN/Optima/CustomCostDimensions.htm)
for more details.

A tag dimension derives its value from specific resource tags.

However, resources might not always be consistently tagged.
For instance, while one set of resources might use the tag `"env"`, another might use `"environment"`.
To handle such inconsistencies, a tag dimension offers flexibility, supporting multiple tag keys.

In this case, by creating an `Environment` tag dimension that lists both `"env"` and `"environment"` tag keys,
the system will extract values from either of these tags to populate the `Environment` dimension,
ensuring comprehensive coverage irrespective of the tagging variations.
And if a resource has multiple matching tags, the value from the earliest listed tag key will be given precedence.

This tag dimension configuration applies to all bill months.
Any changes to the configuration will be reflected in all billing data, past and present, within 24 hours.
